name: dGonpa dialect of mBrugchu Tibetan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Suzuki, Hiroyuki. 2015. Esquisse phonétique du tibétain de dGonpa: un dialecte parlé à mBrugchu. Revue d'Etudes Tibétaines 33 (octobre 2015): 231-249.
catalog_locator: sec. 4 'Traits suprasegmentaux', p. 246 (last two paragraphs before '5. Conclusion') of the RET 33 offprint; saved
catalog_quote: Toutefois, la valeur de la hauteur varie souvent, et on peut prononcer un mot en montant ou en descendant selon l’environnement constitué par les autres syllabes éventuelles ou par les autres sons de la phrase. Autrement dit, aucune frontière lexicale n’existe au-delà de laquelle l’effet de changement de hauteur se produit. ... En règle générale, la hauteur ne descend pas en milieu de phrase. ... la courbe descendante n’est de toute façon pas distinctive d’un point de vue phonologique. On peut donc conclure qu’il n’existe quasiment pas de distinction de hauteur si l’on ne prend pas en compte la phonation spécifique de chaque registre. Le registre dépend toujours de l’initiale, donc le système suprasegmental a théoriquement un statut problématique dans le parler de dGonpa, où la distinction entre les registres n’est pas toujours strictement exprimée. L’accentuation n’apparaît par aucun trait spécifique et phonétiquement évident, hormis l’affaiblissement occasionnel des syllabes situées en deuxième position. Celui-ci consiste en un changement de la position articulatoire de la voyelle, en principe associé à une descente de la hauteur.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: One can thus conclude that there is practically no pitch distinction if one does not take into account the specific phonation of each register. The register always depends on the initial, so the suprasegmental system theoretically has a problematic status in the dGonpa variety, where the distinction between registers is not always strictly expressed. Accentuation (stress) does not show up through any specific, phonetically evident feature, apart from the occasional weakening of syllables in second position. This consists of a change in the articulatory position of the vowel, in principle associated with a drop in pitch.

new_statements.rule_in_words: dGonpa mBrugchu Tibetan has no tone and no phonologically or phonetically salient word stress; suprasegmental behaviour reduces to two phonation registers (plain vs breathy) predictable from the initial consonant. The only prominence asymmetry reported is a weak trochaic tendency: second syllables are occasionally reduced (vowel centralisation with lower pitch), and (Suzuki 2013 fn. 19, 2014 fn. 15) the first syllable of a polysyllabic word tends to be pronounced long, length being non-contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: Occasional weakening of second-position syllables (vowel quality change with pitch lowering); pitch of a word varies with position in the phrase ('la hauteur ne descend pas en milieu de phrase'); the [52] vs [55] contour difference on isolated monosyllables (e.g. 'horse' vs 'now') is judged non-distinctive.
new_statements.domain_note: Description based on elicited words and short sentences from one speaker (dGonpa village, recorded in Chengdu 2012); the accent remark concerns the word (disyllables), while the pitch discussion explicitly notes phrase-level conditioning. Suzuki's own survey classification (SAG VII 2017 p. 13) lists dGonpa and Ongsum Tibetan as 'NT/NA' = no tone / no accent.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement is from Suzuki's sketch of the dGonpa (Gongba 拱壩) dialect of mBrugchu Tibetan = Glottolog dialect dgon1234 under hbru1241 (one speaker from Lhayul hamlet, dGonpa village, recorded in Chengdu 2012). Suzuki 2014 (Ongsum/Baleng 八楞 dialect, the other main subgroup, probably = Glottolog Thergyud ther1234) reports the same picture (no phonological suprasegmentals; first syllable of polysyllables tends to be long) but has no explicit accent sentence. Suzuki argues that earlier Chinese 'Zhouqu dialect' tone data (Huang Bufan 2007, Zhang 1996/2009) actually describe Luoda, now in Thewo County (Thewo-smad, not Drugchu).
